parcel.note: Class-B (non-combustible) construction, unlike the wood-frame Class D of most parcels documented here. The assessor records year built as 1911; the prompting article gives 1912.

assessment.note: No sale on the current roll. Improvements are assessed at more than twice the land value — the reverse of the usual Pacific Heights pattern, reflecting the scale of the building.

notable_residents_omitted.note: The prompting article names a current resident of this house. Under this site's privacy rules — which bar naming or alluding to current occupants, publicly available or not — that claim is omitted. Past, dated residency tied to a published source may be added later.

narrative.lead: The Spreckels Mansion fills a 45,006-square-foot Pacific Heights block — the largest lot and the largest building documented on this site. Recorded in the SF Planning survey as the Spreckels Residence, it is the only individually landmarked building among these pages.

sections.heading: Historic status
sections.body: The article that prompted this page states San Francisco Landmark No. 197, designated 9 June 1990. The city's per-parcel historic dataset confirms the building's Article 10 individual-landmark status and its Category A / A* rating, but does not carry the landmark number or the designation date — so those two figures are the article's, not the city's, and are noted here as unverified against the landmark ordinance itself.

sections.heading: Permit history
sections.body: Eight permits, 1990–2004, one a sidewalk filing. The record clusters in 1990–91: a $600,000 kitchen-and-two-bath remodel, the re-hanging of the iron driveway gate, and — after the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake — a proposal to brace the parapet with steel angles, which expired.

sections.heading: Assessed value
sections.body: Improvements are carried at more than twice the land value — the reverse of the usual Pacific Heights split, and a measure of the building. No sale appears on the current roll.
